title: I was just passing the time of day with old Troy of the D. M. P. at the corner of Arbour hill there and be damned but a bloody sweep came along and he near drove his gear into my eye.
html_source:
Joyce opens the chapter, and continues throughout, with puns on ‘I’/‘Eye’ – playing on the Cyclops' single eye, and his eventual unfortunate encounter with a giant, sharpened piece of olive wood, hidden under some dung in Homer’s Odyssey.

Arbour Hill, incidentally, is a street in Stoneybatter, Dublin, that was renowned for its colourful characters and sharp wit, to say nothing of its famous jail and prostitutes.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: Old Troy had been an official with the Dublin Metropolitan Police (D.M.P.). “Old Troy” is also a reference to the site of the Trojan War where Odysseus plays a prominent role, especially with respect to the huge, hollow horse, whereby he and his men gain access within the walls of the city. Could it be that Odysseus/Bloom, as the sweep, is trying, at this point, to enter “Troy” with only traditional tools and strategies, as with brooms and ladders, as the narrator complains of when the sweep and his equipment are “obstructing the thoroughfare" shortly below?
